sections.b: Chronicles gives Uzziah a full chapter. He seeks God while Zechariah instructs him, and God helps him against the Philistines, Arabs and Meunites (2 Chronicles 26:5–7). He builds towers, digs cisterns and loves farming (2 Chronicles 26:9–10), and his army is equipped with ingenious machines on the walls (2 Chronicles 26:15). Then, "once he was strong, his heart rose up high," and he enters the temple to burn incense, a priestly task. Azariah the priest and eighty others stand against him; as he rages, skin disease breaks out on his forehead, and he lives apart until his death, cut off from the LORD's house (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). Chronicles plays on his two names, Uzziah ("the LORD is my strength") and Azariah ("the LORD has helped"), in the words "help" and "strong" that run through the chapter. A stone plaque from the Second Temple period records the reburial of his bones.

common: Uzziah's skin disease was a punishment for taking on the priests' role by burning incense.
uncommon: Some historians think the incense story was told to explain why a good king was struck with disease, which Kings leaves unexplained.

claude.title: Strength as the danger
claude.body: Claude's reading. Chronicles' Uzziah story reads like a warning written for the successful. Every word for help and strength in the chapter builds toward the turn in 2 Chronicles 26:16, so that the reader feels the moment the gift becomes the snare. The story is less about ritual rules than about a man who could no longer accept a limit. Japhet (1993) and Klein (2012) both trace the 'help' and 'strength' wordplay; the stress on limits is mine.

sections.b: Chronicles ends with Cyrus. After the seventy years of the land's rest, "the LORD roused the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia" to proclaim that the God of the heavens had given him all the kingdoms of the earth and charged him to build a house in Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 36:22–23). The last words invite any of God's people to "go up." The same decree opens Ezra, where it continues with the building of the temple (Ezra 1:1–4). The Cyrus Cylinder shows a similar policy of returning peoples and gods, though it does not mention Judah.

common: Cyrus allowed the Jews to return from Babylon and rebuild the temple in 538 BC.
uncommon: Some historians think the biblical wording of the decree was shaped by Jewish writers, since Persian kings framed such decrees in terms of the local god.

sections.b: Chronicles explains the exile in one sentence: it was to fulfill the LORD's word by Jeremiah "until the land had made up for its Sabbaths. All the days it lay desolate it rested, to fill up seventy years" (2 Chronicles 36:21). This joins Jeremiah's seventy years (Jeremiah 25:11; Jeremiah 29:10) with Leviticus 26:34–35, where a land left desolate rests for the Sabbath years its people did not keep. The result is a picture of an empty land waiting for its people, though Kings and Jeremiah show that some remained (2 Kings 25:12; Jeremiah 40:7–12). The next verse begins the return under Cyrus (2 Chronicles 36:22).

common: The seventy years ran from the first deportation in 605 BC to the return in 538 or 536 BC (the usual traditional Christian count), or from the temple's fall in 586 BC to its rebuilding in 516 BC.
uncommon: Many scholars treat seventy as a round figure for a lifetime of judgment, comparing an inscription of Esarhaddon in which Marduk wrote seventy years for Babylon's desolation and then turned the tablet over to make it eleven.
The Talmud works through the count and has Belshazzar and Ahasuerus each miscount the seventy years, with disastrous results (Bavli Megillah 11b–12a).

sections.b: The last chapters of Chronicles test its teaching most sharply. Amaziah's troubles begin "from the time Amaziah turned away from following the LORD" (2 Chronicles 25:27); Uzziah's disease follows his pride (2 Chronicles 26:16–21); Jotham grows strong because he kept his ways steady (2 Chronicles 27:6); Ahaz is defeated on every side (2 Chronicles 28:5–19). Then the pattern is bent. Sennacherib attacks "after these things and this faithfulness" (2 Chronicles 32:1), and the attack becomes a test. Manasseh, the worst of kings, repents and is restored (2 Chronicles 33:12–13), where Kings blames him for the exile itself (2 Kings 24:3–4). Josiah, the best, dies for not listening to God's word through Neco (2 Chronicles 35:22). At the end the blame rests on Zedekiah's generation, who mocked the prophets "till there was no cure" (2 Chronicles 36:16). Raymond Dillard and others note that the book's rewards are real but that its main concern is the call to return, the promise that if "my people ... humble themselves and pray" (2 Chronicles 7:14).

common: Chronicles shows God rewarding and punishing kings within their own lifetimes.
uncommon: Some read Chronicles' pattern less as a doctrine than as preaching: each story is an invitation to repent, not a rule that all suffering is deserved.

sections.b: In the last twelve chapters, Chronicles both copies Kings word for word and departs from it sharply. It adds Amaziah's hired northern troops and his Edomite gods (2 Chronicles 25:5–16), Uzziah's sin in the temple (2 Chronicles 26:16–21), Hezekiah's temple cleansing and Passover (29–31), Manasseh's captivity and repentance (2 Chronicles 33:11–17), Josiah's early reform and the words of Neco (2 Chronicles 34:3–7; 2 Chronicles 35:21–22). It leaves out much: Hezekiah's tribute (2 Kings 18:14–16), most of Isaiah's oracles, the death of Gedaliah, and the release of Jehoiachin (2 Kings 25:22–30). Some differences are copying slips (Jehoiachin's age, 2 Chronicles 36:9), some the use of a different Kings text, and many the Chronicler's own choices. Chronicles often assumes its readers know Kings (2 Chronicles 32:24, 2 Chronicles 32:31).

common: Chronicles was written after the exile, using Samuel and Kings as its main source.
uncommon: A few scholars, such as A. Graeme Auld, argue that Kings and Chronicles both drew on a shared older text rather than Chronicles copying Kings.

sections.b: Chronicles gives three chapters to what Kings tells in one verse: Hezekiah's reform. In his first month he opens the temple doors his father had shut, has the Levites cleanse it in sixteen days, and rededicates it with sin offerings for all Israel and with David's music (2 Chronicles 29:3–36). He invites the north to a Passover in the second month, prays for the unclean who eat it, and the joy is the greatest since Solomon (2 Chronicles 30:1–27). Gifts pile up in heaps for the priests and Levites (2 Chronicles 31:5–10). Only then does Sennacherib come, after "this faithfulness" (2 Chronicles 32:1). Hezekiah blocks the springs, builds walls and encourages the people, and together with Isaiah he prays; the angel strikes the Assyrian camp (2 Chronicles 32:2–22). His pride after his healing is noted, and his humbling (2 Chronicles 32:25–26). Chronicles leaves out his tribute and the Babylonian envoys' tour, mentioning the envoys only as God's test (2 Chronicles 32:31).

common: Hezekiah was a reforming king who trusted God when Assyria attacked.
uncommon: Some historians doubt that Hezekiah's Passover for all Israel took place, and see it as modeled on Josiah's.

sections.b: Chronicles repeats Kings' list of Manasseh's sins (2 Chronicles 33:1–9) but then tells what Kings does not: the Assyrian officers take him with hooks to Babylon; there he humbles himself, prays, and God hears and restores him to Jerusalem; he removes the foreign gods, rebuilds the LORD's altar and strengthens the city (2 Chronicles 33:10–17). Kings, by contrast, makes Manasseh's sins the reason Judah could not escape exile (2 Kings 21:10–16; 2 Kings 23:26; 2 Kings 24:3–4). No Assyrian record mentions his arrest, though his loyalty to Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal is recorded, and the story has real parallels. His prayer, mentioned in 2 Chronicles 33:18–19, inspired the Prayer of Manasseh, part of the Orthodox Bible and of the Protestant Apocrypha, and a different prayer found at Qumran (4Q381). Rabbis debated whether he has a share in the world to come (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:2).

common: Chronicles presents Manasseh as the worst king who repented and was forgiven.
uncommon: Some historians judge the story of Manasseh's captivity a theological creation to explain his very long reign.

claude.title: Two honest endings
claude.body: Claude's reading. Kings and Chronicles each tell the truth about Manasseh from where they stand. Kings, written in the shadow of the exile, sees the long damage one reign could do to a nation. Chronicles, written for people trying to start again, needs to know whether one man's turning can still matter. Reading both keeps either from becoming cheap: grace is real, and so are consequences. Japhet (The Ideology of the Book of Chronicles) and Williamson (1982) explain the difference by the two books' settings in a similar way; the pastoral framing is mine.

sections.b: Chronicles has Josiah seek God at sixteen and begin purging Judah at twenty, before the law scroll is found in his eighteenth year (2 Chronicles 34:3–8). After Huldah's word and the covenant, the book gives most of its space to his Passover, the finest since Samuel (2 Chronicles 35:1–19). Then Neco marches north, warns Josiah that God has sent him, and Josiah, "disguised" like Ahab, ignores "Neco's words from God's mouth" and is shot at Megiddo; he dies in Jerusalem and is mourned by Jeremiah and the singers (2 Chronicles 35:20–25). 1 Esdras 1 retells these events and has Josiah ignore the words of Jeremiah instead.

common: Josiah died because he went to war against Pharaoh Neco without God's approval.
uncommon: Some scholars think Josiah was not killed in battle at all, but executed at a meeting with Neco, as 2 Kings 23:29 may suggest.

sections.b: Chronicles describes two great Passovers. Hezekiah's is held in the second month, because priests and people were not ready, and is open to the north; many eat it unclean, and Hezekiah prays for them (2 Chronicles 30:1–27). Josiah's is held on the right day, with the Levites slaughtering for all and the king giving thousands of animals (2 Chronicles 35:1–19). Both show the feast becoming a temple sacrifice, with blood splashed on the altar (2 Chronicles 30:16; 2 Chronicles 35:11). Chronicles joins two laws, the roasting of Exodus 12:9 and the "cooking" of Deuteronomy 16:7, in one phrase: "They cooked the Passover in the fire" (2 Chronicles 35:13).

common: Hezekiah and Josiah restored Passover after long neglect.
uncommon: Some scholars think Hezekiah's second-month date reflects a northern calendar, so that northerners could take part.

sections.h: The fall of Jerusalem in Chronicles
sections.b: Chronicles tells the end briefly. Four kings in twenty-two years are deported or removed; the temple vessels go to Babylon in stages (2 Chronicles 36:7, 2 Chronicles 36:10, 2 Chronicles 36:18). The cause is named: the priests and people polluted the temple and mocked the prophets God sent "early and often," until there was no cure (2 Chronicles 36:14–16). The Chaldean king kills even in the sanctuary, burns the temple and takes the survivors to Babylon "until Persia's kingdom began to reign" (2 Chronicles 36:17–20). Chronicles does not tell of Gedaliah or the people left in the land; it presents the land as resting for seventy years (2 Chronicles 36:21), and ends with Cyrus' call to go up (2 Chronicles 36:23).

common: Chronicles blames the exile on the unfaithfulness of the last generation in Judah.
uncommon: Hans Barstad and others argue that the picture of an empty land is theological, since many Judeans remained.

sections.b: Babylon appears first as a friend: its officials send envoys to Hezekiah about the sign (2 Chronicles 32:31). Manasseh is taken there by Assyrian officers, perhaps after the Babylonian revolt of 652–648 BC (2 Chronicles 33:11). Then Nebuchadnezzar comes against Jehoiakim, takes Jehoiachin and the temple's treasures, and at last burns Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 36:6–19). The exiles serve him and his sons until Persia rises (2 Chronicles 36:20).

Ahaz asks the king of Assyria for help, and Tilgath-pilneser "pressed him hard and did not strengthen him" (2 Chronicles 28:16–21). Hezekiah resists Sennacherib, who boasts that no god could save its people; the LORD sends an angel, and Sennacherib goes home in shame to be killed in his god's temple (2 Chronicles 32:1–22). Manasseh is led away by Assyria's officers (2 Chronicles 33:11). Josiah dies opposing Neco, who was marching to Assyria's aid (2 Chronicles 35:20).

These chapters show the northern tribes as part of Israel even after Samaria fell. A prophet of the north, Oded, rebukes Israel's army and its leaders send Judah's captives home with food and clothing (2 Chronicles 28:9–15). Hezekiah invites Ephraim, Manasseh, Asher, Issachar and Zebulun to his Passover, and some come (2 Chronicles 30:1–11, 2 Chronicles 30:18). Josiah's reform reaches the towns of Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon and Naphtali, and the temple repairs are paid with silver from "all the rest of Israel" (2 Chronicles 34:6–9). For Chronicles the twelve tribes are never wholly lost.

In 2 Chronicles 28:9–15 the northern army brings 200,000 captives from Judah to Samaria. The prophet Oded and four Ephraimite leaders insist that they be freed: they clothe the naked, give them sandals, food and drink, anoint them with oil, carry the weak on donkeys and bring them to Jericho. Many readers see this story behind Jesus' parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:30–37), where a Samaritan does the same for a stranger on the Jericho road.

When King Uzziah enters the temple to burn incense on the incense altar, the priests tell him it belongs only to Aaron's descendants (2 Chronicles 26:16–18), as the Law warned after Korah's rebellion (Numbers 16:40). He is struck with skin disease as he holds the censer. Under Ahaz the incense stops (2 Chronicles 29:7), and Hezekiah calls the Levites to restore it (2 Chronicles 29:11).

The Hebrew verb kana', "humble oneself," tells the story of these chapters. Northerners humble themselves and come to Hezekiah's Passover (2 Chronicles 30:11); Hezekiah humbles himself after his pride (2 Chronicles 32:26); Manasseh humbles himself greatly in Babylon and is restored (2 Chronicles 33:12, 2 Chronicles 33:19); Amon does not (2 Chronicles 33:23); Josiah's heart is soft and he humbles himself on hearing the law (2 Chronicles 34:27); Zedekiah will not humble himself before Jeremiah (2 Chronicles 36:12). Hezekiah's letter turns on another verb, shuv, "return": if you return to the LORD, he will return to you (2 Chronicles 30:6–9). The book's promise is God's word to Solomon, that if "my people ... humble themselves and pray" (2 Chronicles 7:14), he will hear.

sections.h: The end of the Hebrew Bible
sections.b: In most printed Hebrew Bibles and in the Talmud's order (Bavli Bava Batra 14b), Chronicles is the last book, so the Hebrew Bible ends with Cyrus' words, "let him go up" (2 Chronicles 36:23). Some medieval codices, such as Aleppo and Leningrad, put it first among the Writings. Christian Bibles, following the Greek, place it after Kings. The Prayer of Manasseh, inspired by 2 Chronicles 33:18–19, is in the Orthodox canon and among the Apocrypha of other churches. Jesus' words about the blood "from Abel to Zechariah" (Luke 11:51) may assume a Bible that began with Genesis and ended with Chronicles (2 Chronicles 24:20–22).

sections.h: 1 Esdras and the Greek of 2 Chronicles 35–36
sections.b: The last two chapters of Chronicles survive in three ancient forms: the Hebrew, the Greek translation of Chronicles, and 1 Esdras, a Greek book that begins with Josiah's Passover and runs on into Ezra. The Greek of Chronicles adds verses drawn from Kings at 2 Chronicles 35:19 and 36:2–5. 1 Esdras has its own differences, such as Josiah ignoring "the words of Jeremiah the prophet" rather than Neco (1 Esdras 1:26), and gives Jehoiachin's age as eight in Codex Vaticanus but eighteen in Codex Alexandrinus (1 Esdras 1:41). Zipora Talshir argued that 1 Esdras was translated from a Hebrew text of its own.

sections.h: Music in Hezekiah's and Josiah's reforms
sections.b: Hezekiah stations the Levites with cymbals, harps and lyres "by the command of David, of Gad ... and of Nathan," and the song of the LORD begins at the moment the burnt offering does (2 Chronicles 29:25–28). They praise "with the words of David and of Asaph the visionary" (2 Chronicles 29:30). Under Josiah, musician Levites oversee the temple builders (2 Chronicles 34:12), and the singers keep their posts through the Passover (2 Chronicles 35:15). Jeremiah and the singers lament Josiah (2 Chronicles 35:25).

Chronicles says Ahaz "burned his sons in the fire" in the Valley of Ben-hinnom (2 Chronicles 28:3), where Kings says he "made his son pass through the fire" (2 Kings 16:3), and Manasseh too made his sons pass through the fire there (2 Chronicles 33:6). The verb in 2 Chronicles 28:3 differs by one letter from Kings', and the Greek of Chronicles follows Kings. Jeremiah later names the same valley as the place where children were burned (Jeremiah 7:31).

Chronicles tells how Josiah went out against Neco and fought "in the valley of Megiddo," where archers wounded him (2 Chronicles 35:22–23). Mourning for him became a custom (2 Chronicles 35:25), and Zechariah compares a future grief to "the mourning ... in the plain of Megiddo" (Zechariah 12:11). This memory of a king's death in battle lies in the background of Revelation's Armageddon, the gathering place of the kings for the last battle.

When Uzziah raged against the priests, tsara'at broke out on his forehead before their eyes, and they hurried him out of the temple (2 Chronicles 26:19–20). He lived in a house set apart until his death, cut off from the LORD's house, and was buried in a field near the royal tombs "for they said, 'He has a skin disease'" (2 Chronicles 26:21–23). The forehead was where the high priest wore the gold plate engraved "Holy to the LORD" (Exodus 28:36–38).
